claims.text: Textile dyeing traditionally relied on natural dyes extracted from plants, insects or minerals.
claims.label: natural dyes from plants and insects

claims.text: Modern textile dyeing predominantly uses synthetic dyes, which offer a broader range of colours, greater colorfastness and easier application.
claims.label: the shift to synthetic dyes

claims.text: The fabric is prepared first, usually by scouring away impurities and oils that would interfere with dye uptake.
claims.label: scouring the fabric first

claims.text: The fabric is then immersed in a dye bath containing the dye, a mordant that helps the dye bind to the fibre, and auxiliary chemicals.
claims.label: the dye bath and its mordant

claims.text: Temperature, pH and the duration of immersion are carefully controlled to give even dye penetration and good colour development.
claims.label: controlled temperature, pH and time

claims.text: Different dye classes such as direct, reactive and vat dyes suit different fibre types and give different levels of wash and light fastness.
claims.label: direct, reactive and vat dyes

claims.text: After dyeing, rinsing and fixation remove excess dye and bond the rest permanently to the textile.
claims.label: rinsing and fixation
